la:noun:barbaria.html:
barbărĭa, ae (poet., or in post-Aug. prose barbărĭes, acc. -em; so once in ), f.
barbarus
.
Lit., a foreign country, in opposition to Greece or Rome.
In gen.: a quo (philosopho) non solum Graecia et Italia, sed etiam omnis barbaria commota est,; ; ; cf.: non solum cum exercitu suo, sed etiam cum omni inmanitate barbariae bellum inferre nobis. ; : quid tibi barbariem. gentes ab utroque jacentes Oceano numerem?: in mediā vivere barbarie,; ; —
Esp., of a particular country, aside from Greece or Rome. Thus (in the mouth of a Greek), of Italy, as opp. to Greece (only in Plaut.), ; id. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. vapula, p. 278.

—Of Persia: Themistoclem non in Graeciae portus, sed in barbariae sinus confugisse,.—Of Phrygia: Graecia barbariae lento collisa duello,.—Of Gaul, in opp. to Rome, (16, 34).—Of Scythia and Britain, ; in gen.: quae barbaria Indiā vastior aut agrestior?—

Meton., mental or moral barbarism, according to the notion of the ancients.
Rudeness, rusticity, stupidity: barbaria forensis,: grandis,.—Hence of barbarism in language: omnes tum fere, qui nec extra urbem hanc vixerant, nec eos aliqua barbaries domestica infuscaverat, recte loquebantur,.—And of faulty reading, .—
Savageness, barbarousness, rudeness, uncivilized manners: inveterata barbaria,: ferum et immane facinus, quod nulla barbaria posset agnoscere,: ista vero quae et quanta barbaria est,; 11, 2, 6: tanta barbaries (Sarmatorum) est, ut pacem non intellegant,; ; ; .—
= barbari: quale bellum nulla umquam barbaria cum suā gente gessit,; cf.: hoc poëtae nomen, quod nulla umquam barbaria violavit,.

Bacchus, i, m., = Βάκχος,
son of Jupiter and a Theban woman, Semele, ; : bis genitus (since, as Semele died before his birth, he was carried about by Jupiter in his hip until the time of his maturity),, ; cf. , and bimatris, ; v. also ; ; the god of wine (as such also called Liber, the deliverer, Lyæus (λύειν), the care-dispeller; cf. Enn. ap. P., or Trag. Rel. v. 149 Vahl.; cf ; as intoxicating and inspiring, he is god of poets, esp. of the highly inspired, ; ; ; ; ; who wore crowns of ivy, which was consecrated to him,: Bacchica verba (poëtae), id .—He was worshipped esp. in Thrace and Macedonia, and particularly upon Mount Edon, ; hence, the Bacchæ are called matres Edonides,; ; v. also Liber.—Bacchus, in the most ancient times, is represented as a god of nature by a Phallic Herma (v. such a statue in O. Müll. Denkm. 4); in the class. per. in the form of a beautiful youth (; ), with a crown of vine leaves or ivy upon his head, and sometimes with small horns upon his forehead (; ; ); hence, corymbifer,; ; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. cornua, p. 37 Müll.; his soft hair fell in long ringlets upon his shoulders (depexus crinibus,; cf. ); with the exception of a fawn's skin (νεβρίς) thrown around him, he was usually represented naked, but with high and beautiful buskins, the Dionysian cothurni, upon his feet; in his hand he, as well as his attendants (a satyr, Silenus, and the Bacchæ), carried the thyrsus (; cf. ); cf. O. Müll. Arch. § 383.—

la:adj:barbarus.html:
barbărus, a, um (
gen. plur. m. barbarum, ; ), adj., = βάρβαρος [cf. barrio; balo, balbus; blatio].
Prop., foreign, strange, barbarous, opp. to Greek or Roman.
In gen.: hospes,: mixta facit Graiis barbara turba metum,; : reges,.—Hence, in Tac., in barbarum, adverb., in the manner or according to the custom of foreigners or barbarians: civitas potens, neque in barbarum corrupta,; .— As subst.: barbărus, i, m., a foreigner, stranger, barbarian: sin hoc et ratio doctis et necessitas barbaris praescripsit,; ; : quo neque noster adit quisquam, nec barbarus audet,: quippe simul nobis habitat discrimine nullo Barbarus,: barbarorum soli prope Germani singulis uxoribus contenti,: barbari praestabant non modicam humanitatem,.—
Esp., of a particular people, in opp. to Greek or Roman or both; cf.: Romanus Graiusque ac barbarus induperator, (cf.: barbaria, barbaricus, and Fest. s. v. barbari, p. 36 Müll.).
(In the mouth of a Greek, or in opp. to Greek.) Italian, Roman, Latin (never so used by the Romans): nam os columnatum poetae esse inaudivi barbaro (sc. Naevio) (words of the Ephesian Periplectomenes),; : i, stultior es barbaro Poticio,: absurdum erat aut tantum barbaris casibus Graecam litteram (φ) adhibere, aut recto casu Graece loqui, .—So also,
In the mouth of a Macedonian: cum alienigenis, cum barbaris aeternum omnibus Graecis bellum est eritque,.—And,
In reference to the inhabitants of Pontus: barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intellegor ulli,.—
Phrygian: tibia,; cf. Forbig.: sonante mixtum tibiis carmen lyrae, Hac Dorium, illis barbarum,; ; .—
Persian, a Persian: solere reges barbaros Persarum ac Syrorum pluris uxores habere,; ; ; ; ; ; . 2.—Thus the king of the Persians is called barbarus, ; ; and high officers of the king, barbari,; cf.: Romanum agmen ad similitudinem barbari incessus convertere,.—
In gen., for any hostile people (among the Romans, after the Aug. age, esp. the German tribes, as, among the Greeks, after the Persian war, the Persians): opinio, quae animos gentium barbararum pervaserat,; ; of the Gauls, ; the Germans, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : ut sunt fluxioris fidei barbari,; the Thracians, ; ; ; Carthaginians, ; Cilicians, ; Phœnicians and Cyprians, ; Parthians, ; ; ; Africans, ; ; ; ; Britons, ; 12, 35; 14, 32; even of the Dassaretians, a Greek people, ; while the Romans did not elsewhere use barbarus for Greek.—
Transf., foreign, strange, in mind or character.
In mind, uncultivated, ignorant; rude, unpolished: qui aliis inhumanus ac barbarus, isti uni commodus ac disertus videretur,: ecqua civitas est... aut tam potens aut tam libera aut etiam tam inmanis ac barbara, etc.,, § 24: nationes,; : Maroboduus... natione magis quam ratione barbarus,.—Comp., of verses: non sunt illa suo barbariora loco,.—
Of character, wild, savage, cruel, barbarous: neque tam barbari linguā et natione illi, quam tu naturā et moribus,: immanis ac barbara consuetudo hominum immolandorum, (10, 21); ; : gens,: homines,: homo,, § 148: pirata,: praedones,; : tollite barbarum Morem,, 27, 2: Medea,: domina,: libidines,: ignis,: populus,.— * Comp.: sacra barbariora,.— Sup. not in use.—Hence, adv.: barbărē.
Prop., as a foreigner would, in a foreign tongue: Demophilus scripsit; Marcus vortit barbare,i. e. into Latin,; ; cf. barbarus, I. B. 1. —
Transf.
Rudely, ignorantly, in an uncultivated way: si grammaticum se professus quispiam barbare loqueretur,: ut is, a quo insolenter quid aut minaciter aut crudeliter dictum sit, barbare locutus existimetur,: tota saepe theatra et omnem Circi turbam exclamasse barbare scimus,.—
Rudely, roughly, barbarously, cruelly: dulcia barbare Laedentem oscula,: ferociter et barbare facere,.
